sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Cloud migration means moving applications, workloads, or data between environments.
Migration is not always on premises to cloud. CompTIA also includes cloud to on premises and cloud to cloud.
Before anything moves, the organization must evaluate whether its resources, applications, costs, network, compliance requirements, and operational model will still work in the destination.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: What is moving, where is it going, and how much should the application change during the move?
sections.callout: Source + destination + amount of application change → determine the migration approach.

entries.title: On-Premises-to-Cloud
paragraphs: This migration moves workloads from infrastructure controlled locally by the organization into a cloud environment.
Think: Our data center → cloud.
entries.recognitionCue: If existing local infrastructure is being moved into cloud services → think on-premises-to-cloud migration.

entries.title: Cloud-to-On-Premises
paragraphs: This moves workloads from a cloud environment back to infrastructure operated by the organization.
Reasons might include changes in cost, control, compatibility, or regulatory requirements.
Think: Bring it back home.
entries.recognitionCue: If a workload is leaving the cloud for company-controlled infrastructure → think cloud-to-on-premises migration.

entries.title: Cloud-to-Cloud
paragraphs: This migration moves a workload between cloud environments.
Think: Cloud A → Cloud B.
entries.recognitionCue: If the workload is moving between cloud environments or providers → think cloud-to-cloud migration.

sections.title: Resource Allocation
paragraphs: Before migration, the organization needs to determine the compute, storage, network, and supporting resources required in the destination environment.
Allocating too little can cause poor performance. Allocating far too much can increase cost unnecessarily.
Think: Move the workload, not the old waste.
sections.callout: If the migration requires determining how much destination capacity the workload needs → think resource allocation.

entries.title: Storage
paragraphs: Determine how much data must move, which storage type the workload needs, how quickly the data can be transferred, and what storage performance the application requires.
entries.recognitionCue: Large data movement or destination storage needs → think storage consideration.

entries.title: Platform Compatibility
paragraphs: The destination must support the application's operating environment, software, services, architecture, and other requirements.
Think: Can this workload actually live there?
entries.recognitionCue: If the destination cannot properly support the application → think platform compatibility.

entries.title: Compute
paragraphs: The new environment must provide enough processing resources for the workload.
Think: Enough CPU and memory for the job.
entries.recognitionCue: If workload processing capacity is the concern → think compute.

entries.title: Cost
paragraphs: Migration itself can cost money, and the new environment has ongoing operating expenses.
Organizations must examine whether the migration actually makes financial sense.
entries.recognitionCue: If the destination works technically but may cost too much → think cost consideration.

entries.title: Networking
paragraphs: Applications may depend on connectivity among users, systems, cloud resources, and other environments.
Migration can change network routes, addresses, bandwidth requirements, and latency.
entries.recognitionCue: If moving the workload changes how systems communicate → think networking consideration.

entries.title: Management Overhead
paragraphs: A migration may reduce or increase the amount of administration required.
Think: Who has to manage this after we move it?
entries.recognitionCue: If staffing or administration requirements change after migration → think management overhead.

entries.title: Service Availability
paragraphs: The organization must plan how migration affects uptime. Some migrations can tolerate extended downtime; others cannot.
entries.recognitionCue: If the business must remain operational during the move → think service availability.

entries.title: Vendor Lock-In
paragraphs: Vendor lock-in occurs when a workload becomes strongly dependent on one provider's technologies or services, making future migration difficult or expensive.
Think: Easy to enter, painful to leave.
entries.recognitionCue: If using a proprietary cloud feature makes switching providers difficult → think vendor lock-in.

entries.title: Environmental — Power and Cooling
paragraphs: Moving workloads can change physical infrastructure requirements.
Moving into cloud services may reduce local equipment needs. Moving back on premises may increase electricity, cooling, and facility-capacity requirements.
entries.recognitionCue: If migration changes physical data-center requirements → think environmental power and cooling.

entries.title: Regulatory
paragraphs: An organization may be legally required to handle systems or data in specific ways.
entries.recognitionCue: If laws or government rules affect where or how the workload can operate → think regulatory requirements.

entries.title: Compliance
paragraphs: Organizations may need to demonstrate that their environment follows required standards, policies, or controls.
entries.recognitionCue: If migration must maintain required standards or controls → think compliance.

sections.title: Application Migration Strategies
paragraphs: This group is extremely recognition-heavy. Focus on how much the application changes and whether it moves at all.

entries.title: Rehost
paragraphs: Rehost means moving an application to the new environment with very little change. This is often called lift and shift.
Think: Pick it up and put it there.
entries.recognitionCue: If the goal is moving quickly without redesigning the application → think rehost.

entries.title: Replatform
paragraphs: Replatform involves making some changes so the application can take better advantage of the destination without completely redesigning it.
Think: Move it and tune it.
entries.recognitionCue: If the application moves mostly intact but receives moderate platform-related improvements → think replatform.

entries.title: Re-Architect
paragraphs: Re-architect means changing the application's overall design or architecture to better support the new environment.
Think: Redesign how the application is built.
entries.recognitionCue: If the migration requires a major architectural redesign → think re-architect.

entries.title: Retain
paragraphs: Retain means keeping the application where it currently resides because migration may be too expensive, too risky, unnecessary, or incompatible.
Think: Leave it alone.
entries.recognitionCue: If the organization decides not to move the workload → think retain.

entries.title: Retire
paragraphs: Retire means removing an application or workload because it is no longer needed.
Think: Turn it off and say goodbye.
entries.recognitionCue: If an obsolete workload should be eliminated instead of migrated → think retire.

entries.title: Refactor
paragraphs: Refactor means modifying application code so it works better with the new environment or architecture.
The business function may remain the same while the internal code is improved or changed.
Think: Rewrite or reorganize the code.
entries.recognitionCue: If developers must significantly change application code → think refactor.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Destination cannot support current workload → Platform compatibility
Cloud service is difficult to leave → Vendor lock-in
Maintain uptime during the move → Service availability
Small or moderate cloud improvements → Replatform
Do not need it anymore → Retire

entries.title: Rehost vs. Replatform
paragraphs: Rehost means almost no application change. Replatform makes some changes to benefit from the new platform.

entries.title: Replatform vs. Re-Architect
paragraphs: Replatform tunes the application. Re-architect redesigns the application's structure.

entries.title: Re-Architect vs. Refactor
paragraphs: These can overlap in the real world. For exam recognition, re-architect emphasizes architecture or design changes; refactor emphasizes code changes.

entries.title: Retain vs. Retire
paragraphs: Retain means keep using the workload where it is. Retire means stop using it entirely.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Determine destination CPU, storage, and network capacity → Resource allocation
Can the destination run the workload? → Platform compatibility
Cloud service makes a provider change difficult → Vendor lock-in
Migration must avoid an outage → Service availability
Physical facility requirements change → Power and cooling
Leave workload where it is → Retain
